title: Mahapajapati Gotami, first Buddhist nun (traditional account)
summary: Mahapajapati Gotami, the Buddha's aunt and foster mother in the Pali tradition, is said to have asked him to admit women to the monastic life, been refused, and then been ordained with other Sakyan women at Vesali after Ananda spoke for her, on condition of accepting eight rules. This is the tradition's account of the founding of the order of nuns.

uncertainty.note: No dated record exists for her ordination. The range spans the Theravada tradition's Buddha dates (623–543 BCE) and the later scholarly placement of his death around 400 BCE; the account itself says only that the request came five years after the Awakening.

as_recorded.value: Five years after the Awakening, the King died and she asked the Buddha to found an order of nuns
Theravada dates 623-543 B.C.E.; many current scholars place his death c. 400 B.C.E.

when.display: Traditional account; the Buddha's own dates are debated (c. 6th–5th century BCE)

where.modern_name: Basarh (Vaishali), Bihar, India, identified as the site of ancient Vesali
where.historical_name: Vesali, capital of the Vajji (Licchavi) confederacy, per the Pali tradition

importance.justification: Tradition credits her with founding the first Buddhist order of women, a landmark in the history of female monasticism.

reviewer_note: Treat as tradition, not history: the story comes from the Pali canon (AN 8.51, Vinaya Cullavagga 10) and later commentary, and I did not open scholarship assessing whether the events, eight rules or Vesali setting are historical. The date range is deliberately wide. AN 8.51 itself was opened only as a SuttaCentral summary; the Vesali setting rests on the Anandajoti page. Pin is modern Basarh, not a specific monastery.
